tables.title: Table 1: Population Size Estimates among Women Engaged in Commercial Sex Using 3-Source Capture Recapture by survey site in Uganda, 2024 – 2025
context: Executive Summary

This report provides findings from a biobehavioral Sentinel Surveillance surveys (BBS) among women engaged in commercial sex (WCS) implemented from 2024 - 2025 by the Crane Survey Project, a collaborative activity of Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH), Ministry of Health (MoH), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with funding from the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). The BSS included 15 sites: Arua, Buliisa, Busia, Buvuma, Fort Portal, Gulu, Hoima, Jinja, Kabale, Kampala, Lira, Masaka, Mbale, Mbarara, Tororo.

The aim of the BSS was to inform HIV programming and policy in Uganda by estimating prevalence of HIV, syphilis, and Human papillomavirus (HPV), HIV service uptake (ART coverage, viral load suppression, and CD4 cell count) and HIV prevention services such as Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), risky behaviors (alcohol use, drug use), depression, and violence against children. The population size of WCS was estimated and this surveillance employed Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS) design. Main findings are summarized in Tables 1-3 below.

A total of 8668 participants were enrolled in the biobehavioral survey across 15 sentinel surveillance sites in Uganda between 2024 and 2025, using respondent-driven sampling. The largest sample was enrolled in Kampala (n≈1,242), followed by Gulu (n≈706) Masaka (n≈661) and Lira (n≈644) sites, the rest of the participants were distributed across Arua, Buliisa, Busia, Buvuma, Fort Portal, Hoima, Jinja, Kabale, Mbale, Mbarara, Tororo sites. The study population included women engaged in commercial sex (WCS). Estimates presented in this report reflect the combined WCS population unless otherwise specified.
Table 1: Population Size Estimates among Women Engaged in Commercial Sex Using 3-Source Capture Recapture by survey site in Uganda, 2024 – 2025

tables.title: Key
context: Initial surveillance survey participants (“seeds”) were gradually recruited by the surveillance team to start enrollment. Seeds were purposively enrolled to reflect a broad array of sociodemographic characteristics (e.g., age, sexual orientation, education, area of residence, marital status, language, religion), HIV status, and affiliation with a PRHIV organization or PRHIV service provider. At the time of their enrollment, seeds were oriented to promote a feeling of ownership and enthusiasm about the project. Seeds were provided with coupons to distribute to their eligible peers for enrollment. Instructions for peer recruitment using an enrollment process script were provided to seeds and participants as detailed in section 2.4.
Sentinel Sites:

Crane Survey offices were located in 15 districts/cities (i.e., Arua, Buliisa, Busia, Buvuma, Fort Portal, Gulu, Hoima, Jinja, Kabale, Kampala, Lira, Masaka, Mbale, Mbarara, Tororo) across the country as shown in the map in Figure 1.
Figure 1: Map of Uganda showing the Crane 4 15 Sentinel Sites located in cities/districts of Uganda

tables.title: Table 1 A: Types of Tests Done, Place and Return Period
context: Laboratory Testing

Laboratory testing was carried out both on-site and off-site. Nearby accredited/certified regional referral hospital laboratories conducted tests for HPV, CD4 count and provided viral load samples and DBS temporary storage. Central Public Health Laboratories (CPHL) was responsible for viral load testing and longer DBS storage. Testing using DBS was done at international laboratories at CDC in Atlanta, USA. Material Transfer Agreements (MTA) were signed to enable sample shipment outside Uganda.
Laboratory Procedures

Participants who were eligible and consented had 10 ml of venous blood drawn into EDTA-containing vacutainer tubes. Blood was stored at room temperature or kept at 2-8°C at nearby peripheral hub and later transported to the CPHL where specimens were tested for HIV and CD4+ T cell counts. Samples (plasma) were prepared and transported for storage at CPHL at -20°C and -80 °C with consent of participants to allow future testing. Sample storage conditions in Entebbe met standard conditions, including daily monitoring of temperature.

Syphilis

Screening: we used DPP syphilis screen and confirm Chembio cassettes to detect both treponema and non-treponema antibodies. This test employs a unique combination of protein A and anti-human immunoglobulin antibody, which are conjugated into colloidal gold particles. It also utilizes a recombinant antigen of T. pallidum and synthetic antigens for non-treponema, separately bound to a membrane solid phase, following the manufacturer’s instructions (Chembio diagnostic systems, INC 3661 Horseblock Road, Medford)

HIV testing

The serological HIV testing method employed serially were Alere Determine HIV- 1/2 rapid test reactive specimens and confirmed with HIV 1/2 Stat-Pak assay. Specimens with discordant Determine – Statpak reactivity were further tested with the SD Bioline Recombigen HIV 1/2 test (tie breaker) following the HIV national testing algorithm/guideline (Figure 3).

tables.title: Table 1 D: Input Parameters and Target Sample Sizes for WCS BBS surveillance surveys, Uganda, 2024-2025
context: Target Sample Size estimation

For surveys with an HIV prevalence of >10%, the target sample size aimed to estimate VLS with a precision of no more than +/- 10 percentage points. Assuming a design effect of 2 in RDS surveys (Salganik et al., 2006, Salganik et al., 2010), this meant that to collect VL results for about 200 participants (see Table 7 below for varying scenarios). Our total target sample size therefore varied between 500 and 1,700 (larger HIV prevalence required smaller sample sizes). Further we monitored convergence and bottleneck graphs for VLS and HIV prevalence (See Annex 6) and would continue sampling (and introduce new seeds) if convergence had not been reached for both indicators or severe bottlenecks are observed
To accommodate still circulating (valid) RDS coupons after coupon issuance had been stopped, the final sample sizes slightly exceeded the needed sample sizes or the maximum sample size stated here.
Table 1 D: Input Parameters and Target Sample Sizes for WCS BBS surveillance surveys, Uganda, 2024-2025

tables.title: Table 2 A: Enrollment Characteristics per Sentinel Site, Uganda, 2024-2025
context: Table 1 D: Input Parameters and Target Sample Sizes for WCS BBS surveillance surveys, Uganda, 2024-2025
Seeds and Enrolment

Seeds were participants who initiated in each referral chain and were purposely selected by the investigators in collaboration with the CBOs. Seed selection prioritized individuals with large social networks, positive community standing, and alignment with surveillance survey objectives. To ensure independence and diversity, seeds were chosen from various backgrounds based on age, place of residence, education, socioeconomic status. Seeds met the respective eligibility criteria and were given coupons and instructions for peer recruitment.

Seeds and subsequent participants received 3 coupons at the beginning of the sentinel surveillance survey and as time progressed, the number of coupons given to recruits per sentinel surveillance survey site depended on the proportion of coupons redeemed to facilitate continued waves and to enable attainment of the desired sampling size. Due to the varying local contexts of these sentinel surveillance survey sites that is, the social economic, cultural diversities of these environments, enrolment and participation in some areas required bigger or greater number of seeds to try and capture higher, diverse respondents or create new waves of participants to obtain the sample size and also sustain the sentinel surveillance survey. The Table 8 below explains participation in terms of duration of the surveillance survey, coupon distribution and eligibility at the 15 sentinel sites.

tables.title: Population Size Estimates using 3-Source Capture Recapture among WCS Surveyed in 15 Sites, Uganda, 2024-2025
context: Ethical Considerations

Prior to the beginning of the surveillance survey, Crane Survey held consultations with the PRHIV community across all the sentinel surveillance survey sites. These were to be involved in the design, implementation, report writing and dissemination phases to ensure inclusivity and relevance. Protocol approval was obtained from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Makerere University School of Public Health (MakSPH) Higher Degrees Research and Ethics Committee (HDREC) Institutional Review Board (IRB), the Population Council IRB, and the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology (UNCST).
Results
Population Size Estimates using 3-Source Capture Recapture among WCS Surveyed in 15 Sites, Uganda, 2024-2025

Between 2024 and 2025, the 3SCRC study estimated the population size of WCS across 15 Sentinel Surveillance sites within Uganda’s districts/cities using both absolute and network-size (SS-PSE) methods. Hoima had the largest estimated number with ~7,621 women (95% CI 4,543–1,1580), together with Kampala (13%), Arua (14.6%), and Hoima (19.8%) having the highest relative proportions. Lira (1.9%), Buvuma (1.9%) and Buliisa (2.1%) had the lowest proportions. Generally, results highlight substantial variation in the size and concentration of WCS populations across the country.

Between 2024 and 2025, the 3SCRC study estimated the population size of WCS across 15 Sentinel Surveillance sites within Uganda’s districts/cities using both absolute and network-size (SS-PSE) methods. Hoima had the largest estimated number with ~7,621 women (95% CI 4,543–1,1580), together with Kampala (13%), Arua (14.6%), and Hoima (19.8%) having the highest relative proportions. Lira (1.9%), Buvuma (1.9%) and Buliisa (2.1%) had the lowest proportions. Generally, results highlight substantial variation in the size and concentration of WCS populations across the country.
Result A: Demographic characteristics

This section presents demographic characteristics across 15 districts in Uganda, showing a predominantly young population with the majority under 35 years old. In pooled data (N=8,304), the weighted median age was 27 years (IQR 23–33); 33.9% were aged 15–24 years and 46.1% were aged 25–34 years. Educational attainment is generally low, with 18.0% reporting no schooling and 36.0% completing some primary education. A particularly striking finding is the high prevalence of homelessness (65.3%) and being divorced, widowed, or separated (51.7%), which together suggest significant social and economic vulnerability. The presence of dependents among most respondents (78.1%), combined with low rates of living with a spouse or partner (19.1%, among those asked), indicates substantial caregiving responsibilities without stable household support.

tables.title: Table B0: Pooled 15 districts: Sexual behavioral characteristics of Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table A14: Mbarara Demographic characteristics of WCS, 2024-2025
Table A15: Tororo Demographic characteristics of WCS, 2024-2025
Result B: Sexual behavioral characteristics

This section shows patterns of violence and exploitation, with substantial proportions experiencing rape, physical abuse, and non-payment by clients. In pooled data (N=8,304), the weighted median age of sex work debut was 21 years (IQR 18–25) and median duration of sex work was 2 years (IQR 0–5). Condom use during the last three sex acts shows mixed patterns: 54.5% reported condom use in all three acts, while 21.0% reported use in two acts, 9.6% in one act, and 14.9% reported no condom use. Anal sex was reported by 15.3% in the past 12 months, and among those, 55.3% used a condom at last anal sex. Experiences of sexual violence were common: 22.4% reported rape/forced sex in the last 12 months and 13.8% more than 12 months ago, with clients frequently identified as perpetrators. Physical abuse was also reported (29.4% in the last 12 months). Economic vulnerability was marked, with 51.9% reporting non-payment/theft by clients in the past 12 months.

tables.title: Table B3: Busia Sexual behavioral characteristics of WCS, 2024-2025
context: This section shows patterns of violence and exploitation, with substantial proportions experiencing rape, physical abuse, and non-payment by clients. In pooled data (N=8,304), the weighted median age of sex work debut was 21 years (IQR 18–25) and median duration of sex work was 2 years (IQR 0–5). Condom use during the last three sex acts shows mixed patterns: 54.5% reported condom use in all three acts, while 21.0% reported use in two acts, 9.6% in one act, and 14.9% reported no condom use. Anal sex was reported by 15.3% in the past 12 months, and among those, 55.3% used a condom at last anal sex. Experiences of sexual violence were common: 22.4% reported rape/forced sex in the last 12 months and 13.8% more than 12 months ago, with clients frequently identified as perpetrators. Physical abuse was also reported (29.4% in the last 12 months). Economic vulnerability was marked, with 51.9% reporting non-payment/theft by clients in the past 12 months.

tables.title: Table C0: Pooled 15 districts-Distribution of stigma related characteristics of Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table B14: Mbarara Sexual behavioral characteristics of WCS, 2024-2025
Table B15: Tororo Sexual behavioral characteristics of WCS, 2024-2025
Result C: Distribution of stigma related characteristics

Healthcare access barriers driven by stigma were reported. In pooled data (N=8,304), 19.8% reported being denied healthcare due to sex work status within the last 12 months and 9.4% reported denial more than 12 months ago. 36.0% reported not feeling comfortable disclosing sex work status to a healthcare worker. Avoidance of healthcare due to concern over possible stigma was common, with 23.8% reporting avoiding care often and 23.7% sometimes, while 52.6% reported no avoidance.

Result D: Self-reported HIV testing history

Over nine in ten respondents reported ever testing for HIV. In pooled data (N=8,304), 93.0% reported ever testing for HIV. Among those ever tested (N=7,767), 30.9% reported their most recent HIV test result was positive, 63.9% negative, and 5.1% unknown. Nearly half reported HIV self-testing within the last 12 months (48.8%) and 58.0% reported testing within the past 12 months. The most common testing venue was hospitals/clinics (57.7%). Among those who had ever tested positive and had a non-paying partner at the time of testing (N=1,252), 33.0% disclosed their result to their partner. Following an HIV positive test, 48.6% reported their partner tested (N=844), and 71.9% reported their children tested (N=1,179). Notable variation existed across districts in testing coverage and self-reported HIV positivity.

tables.title: Table E0: Pooled 15 districts-HIV, syphilis, and HPV burdens among Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table D14: Mbarara Self-reported HIV testing history among WCS, 2024-2025
Table D15: Tororo Self-reported HIV testing history among WCS, 2024-2025
Result E: HIV, syphilis, and HPV burden

HIV prevalence was 31.0% overall, with marked increases by age from 14.3% among those aged 15–24 years to 52.1% among those aged 35–49 years. Among HIV-positive individuals, unsuppressed viral load varied by age, with the highest unsuppressed viral load among 15–24-year-olds (51.5%) compared with 34.3% among 25–34-year-olds and 28.9% among 35–49-year-olds (noting some missing VL results). Active syphilis prevalence was 4.6% overall with minimal age variation. HPV prevalence was 40.7% overall among those tested (N=6,308), declining by age from 49.1% among 15–24-year-olds to 32.2% among 35–49-year-olds. District-level HIV prevalence ranged from 20.6% to 41.7%, while syphilis ranged from 2.0% to 15.0%.

tables.title: Table F0: Pooled 15 districts-Reproductive Health characteristics among Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table E14: Mbarara HIV, syphilis, and HPV burdens among WCS, 2024-2025
Table E15: Tororo HIV, syphilis, and HPV burdens among WCS, 2024-2025
Result F: Reproductive Health characteristics

Among women in commercial sex across 15 districts, 61.3% reported current family planning use, with injectable contraceptives being the most common method (45.1%) followed by implants (22.3%). More than four in five women had ever been pregnant (81.3%), with 49.7% reporting 1–2 pregnancies and 41.8% reporting 3–5 pregnancies. Among those who had been pregnant while selling sex (51.2%), 78.9% received antenatal care, though disclosure of sex work status to ANC providers was low (39.8%). Reported stigma in ANC settings was high (89.6%) among those who received ANC. Among women who received ANC and reported HIV testing during pregnancy (N=2,427), 22.9% reported testing HIV-positive, and among those, 93.7% reported taking ARVs while pregnant. District-level variation was observed, with Arua reporting the lowest family planning use (43.4%) and Fort Portal the highest (72.9%), while pregnancy while selling sex ranged from 31.2% in Buvuma to 64.8% in Mbale.

Result G: HIV outreach services

Approximately three in five women in commercial sex reported exposure to HIV outreach services in the six months preceding the survey (58.7%), with an additional 24.1% exposed more than six months prior and 17.2% never exposed. District-level coverage ranged from 75.3% reporting outreach in the last 6 months in Buvuma to 46.3% in Lira and 46.5% in Buliisa. Among those exposed to outreach (N=6,929), condoms were the most commonly received service (56.9%), followed by HIV testing (42.4%) and HIV information (26.4%), with lubricants received by 12.2%. Substantial district variations were observed in service types received, with Arua and Hoima reporting higher HIV information provision (65.3% and 44.4%, respectively) compared to the pooled estimate, while condom receipt ranged from 41.3% in Gulu to 72.8% in Arua and 72.2% in Buvuma. The proportion never exposed to any outreach was highest in Buliisa (38.9%) and lowest in Buvuma (10.6%).

tables.title: Table H0: Pooled data for 15 districts-Distribution of HIV prevalence by socio-demographic characteristics among Women Living with HIV, who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table G14: Mbarara HIV outreach services accessed by WCS
Table G15: Tororo HIV outreach services accessed by WCS
Result H: HIV prevalence by socio-demographic characteristics

HIV prevalence among women in commercial sex across 15 districts was 31.0%. HIV prevalence increased with age, from 14.3% among 15–24-year-olds to 34.1% among 25–34-year-olds and 52.1% among 35–49-year-olds. District-level HIV prevalence ranged from 20.6% in Buliisa and 21.9% in Arua to 41.7% in Mbarara and 41.4% in Fort Portal. Among HIV-positive women, 96.5% reported an alcohol abuse problem and 63.8% had some or severe depression (with 15.2% undetermined). Among HIV-positive women who had ever used drugs (N=1,018), 35.7% reported injecting in the past 6 months and 14.6% reported injecting more than 6 months ago.

Result J: TB outcomes

Among HIV-positive women who engage in commercial sex (pooled N=2,604), 59.0% reported being screened for TB symptoms, while 13.7% reported not being screened, 5.0% did not remember, and 22.3% did not provide a response. Screening coverage among HIV-positive women varied substantially across districts, ranging from 42.0% in Lira to 70.6% in Arua and 70.2% in Masaka. Among HIV-positive women who were screened (N=1,568), 19.9% reported that no provider talked to them about TB, 13.3% reported being told they had TB, and 66.9% were told they did not have TB. Among HIV-positive women told they had TB (N=207), 91.1% reported receiving TB treatment (district-level treatment coverage ranged from 67.2% in Lira to 100% in several sites, with 88.4% in Fort Portal and 85.7% in Masaka). Overall, missing or unreported screening information was notable in several districts—particularly Kampala (37.6% “Not provided”) and **Lira (34.5% “Not provided”)—**which should be considered when interpreting district comparisons.

tables.title: Table K0: Pooled data for 15 districts-ART characteristics among Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Result K: ART characteristics

Among HIV-positive women in commercial sex (N=2,604), 86.9% reported currently being on ART (district range: 76.7% in Lira to 95.0% in Fort Portal). Among women currently on ART (N=2,289), the most common reported ART provider was hospital/clinic (56.6%), followed by NGOs (16.1%) and drop-in centers (6.9%), though 18.5% did not report a provider type. Just over half (55.0%) reported receiving care from one provider since ART initiation, while 18.2% reported two providers and 8.2% reported three or more, with 18.5% not providing a response.

Nearly one in three women on ART reported missing at least one ART refill in the last 12 months (30.7%), and missed refills were most commonly attributed to being away from home (53.3%) and lack of transportation (23.3%). District variation in missed refills was substantial, ranging from 25.9% in Fort Portal to 39.4% in Mbarara.

Disclosure of sex work status to ART providers was uncommon: 37.2% reported disclosure overall, ranging from 22.0% in Kampala to 58.0% in Arua; 34.7% reported not disclosing, 9.6% were unsure, and 18.5% did not provide a response. Most women reported respectful treatment at their last ART visit (77.4%), though this varied widely across districts (e.g., 92.2% in Arua vs 61.3% in Kampala), and 18.5% did not provide a response in the pooled data. Food insecurity was high among women on ART: 42.6% reported not having enough to eat (vs 38.9% reporting enough; 18.5% no response). District differences were marked, with the highest “not enough to eat” reported in Mbale (60.7%) and Kampala (47.0%).

context: Among HIV-positive women in commercial sex (N=2,604), 86.9% reported currently being on ART (district range: 76.7% in Lira to 95.0% in Fort Portal). Among women currently on ART (N=2,289), the most common reported ART provider was hospital/clinic (56.6%), followed by NGOs (16.1%) and drop-in centers (6.9%), though 18.5% did not report a provider type. Just over half (55.0%) reported receiving care from one provider since ART initiation, while 18.2% reported two providers and 8.2% reported three or more, with 18.5% not providing a response.

Nearly one in three women on ART reported missing at least one ART refill in the last 12 months (30.7%), and missed refills were most commonly attributed to being away from home (53.3%) and lack of transportation (23.3%). District variation in missed refills was substantial, ranging from 25.9% in Fort Portal to 39.4% in Mbarara.

Disclosure of sex work status to ART providers was uncommon: 37.2% reported disclosure overall, ranging from 22.0% in Kampala to 58.0% in Arua; 34.7% reported not disclosing, 9.6% were unsure, and 18.5% did not provide a response. Most women reported respectful treatment at their last ART visit (77.4%), though this varied widely across districts (e.g., 92.2% in Arua vs 61.3% in Kampala), and 18.5% did not provide a response in the pooled data. Food insecurity was high among women on ART: 42.6% reported not having enough to eat (vs 38.9% reporting enough; 18.5% no response). District differences were marked, with the highest “not enough to eat” reported in Mbale (60.7%) and Kampala (47.0%).

tables.title: Table L0: Pooled data for 15 districts- UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets (Conditional and unconditional HIV cascade) of Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table K15: Tororo ART characteristics among WCS, 2024-2025
Result L: UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets (Conditional and unconditional HIV cascade)

HIV prevalence among women who engage in commercial sex across the 15 districts was 31%, ranging from 21% in Arua and Buliisa to 42% in Mbarara and Fort Portal. Among women living with HIV, about nine in ten were aware of their HIV status (pooled 89%), though awareness varied by district from 82% in Buvuma to 96% in Fort Portal. Among those aware of their status, nearly all were on ART (pooled 97%), with ART coverage exceeding 95% in most districts. However, viral suppression among those on treatment was lower than the 95% target (pooled 75%), with substantial district variation ranging from 70% in Lira to 91% in Kabale.

The UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets specify that 95% of people living with HIV should know their status, 95% of those aware should be on ART, and 95% of those on ART should be virally suppressed. The unconditional cascade (measured among all HIV-positive women, regardless of earlier cascade steps) showed 89% aware of status (target: 95%), 86% on ART (target: 90%, reflecting 95% of the 95% who should be aware), and 65% virally suppressed (target: 86%, reflecting 95% × 95% × 95%). Overall, this indicates a ~24 percentage point drop from awareness (89%) to viral suppression (65%) and a 21 percentage point shortfall relative to the 86% viral suppression target implied by 95-95-95. Only three districts—Kabale (83%), Busia (79%), and Fort Portal (73%)—achieved unconditional viral suppression above 70%. The pooled gap is driven primarily by incomplete viral suppression among those on ART, rather than by large gaps in testing/diagnosis or ART coverage.

The unconditional cascade (measured among all HIV-positive women, regardless of earlier cascade steps) showed 89% aware of status (target: 95%), 86% on ART (target: 90%, reflecting 95% of the 95% who should be aware), and 65% virally suppressed (target: 86%, reflecting 95% × 95% × 95%). Overall, this indicates a ~24 percentage point drop from awareness (89%) to viral suppression (65%) and a 21 percentage point shortfall relative to the 86% viral suppression target implied by 95-95-95. Only three districts—Kabale (83%), Busia (79%), and Fort Portal (73%)—achieved unconditional viral suppression above 70%. The pooled gap is driven primarily by incomplete viral suppression among those on ART, rather than by large gaps in testing/diagnosis or ART coverage.

Result M: CD4 count and HIV viral load

Among HIV-positive women in commercial sex, immune status was generally preserved, with a median CD4 count of 702 cells/μL (IQR: 499–923) and 80% in CD4 Stage 1 (≥500 cells/μL). Viral load monitoring was incomplete: 46% reported a viral load test within the past 12 months, while 29% provided no response to the viral load testing question, suggesting substantial gaps in documented monitoring. Among women with viral load results (N=2505), 58% had undetectable viral load (<50 copies/mL), and 83% were suppressed below 1000 copies/mL when combining those <50, 50–199, and 200–999 copies/mL; 17% had viral loads >999 copies/mL. Among respondents who reported receiving viral load results (N=1583), 69% said they understood their results and most preferred receiving results directly from healthcare workers (71%) rather than by text (10%). Awareness of U=U was 46% among respondents asked this item (N=2407). District variation was substantial, with recent viral load testing ranging from 31% in Kampala to 58% in Masaka, and U=U awareness ranging from 33% in Mbarara to 53% in Jinja.

tables.title: Table M3: Busia Viral Load and CD4 count among WCS, 2024-2025
context: Among HIV-positive women in commercial sex, immune status was generally preserved, with a median CD4 count of 702 cells/μL (IQR: 499–923) and 80% in CD4 Stage 1 (≥500 cells/μL). Viral load monitoring was incomplete: 46% reported a viral load test within the past 12 months, while 29% provided no response to the viral load testing question, suggesting substantial gaps in documented monitoring. Among women with viral load results (N=2505), 58% had undetectable viral load (<50 copies/mL), and 83% were suppressed below 1000 copies/mL when combining those <50, 50–199, and 200–999 copies/mL; 17% had viral loads >999 copies/mL. Among respondents who reported receiving viral load results (N=1583), 69% said they understood their results and most preferred receiving results directly from healthcare workers (71%) rather than by text (10%). Awareness of U=U was 46% among respondents asked this item (N=2407). District variation was substantial, with recent viral load testing ranging from 31% in Kampala to 58% in Masaka, and U=U awareness ranging from 33% in Mbarara to 53% in Jinja.

tables.title: Table N0: Pooled data for 15 districts-PrEP knowledge and use among HIV negative Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table M14: Mbarara Viral Load and CD4 count among WCS, 2024-2025
Table M15: Tororo Viral Load and CD4 count among WCS, 2024-2025
Result N: PrEP knowledge and use

Among HIV-negative women engaged in commercial sex, 59% had heard of PrEP (95% CI: 57.6–60.4), with awareness ranging from 37% in Lira to 73% in Buvuma. Among women who had heard of PrEP (N=3441), 58% reported ever being offered PrEP by a healthcare provider (95% CI: 56.4–60.0), and 75% knew where to access it (95% CI: 73.3–76.5). Current PrEP use in the past seven days was 25% among those who had heard of PrEP (95% CI: 23.8–27.0), ranging from 10% in Masaka to 41% in Lira and Arua. Overall, 58% of HIV-negative women expressed a desire to initiate PrEP (95% CI: 56.2–59.1), with district variation from 38% in Lira to 71% in Arua. Among women who had not used PrEP in the past six months (N=2140), the most commonly cited barriers were fear of side effects (23%), limited knowledge about PrEP (22%), and concerns that others may think they have HIV (21%), highlighting the need to strengthen PrEP education and reduce HIV-related stigma alongside PrEP service delivery.

tables.title: Table O0: Pooled data for 15 districts-Alcohol among Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table N14: Mbarara PrEP knowledge and use among HIV negative WCS, 2024-2025
Table N15: Tororo PrEP knowledge and use among HIV negative WCS, 2024-2025
Result O: Alcohol use

Alcohol use was common among women in commercial sex across the 15 districts. In pooled data, 24% reported never drinking alcohol (95% CI: 22.6–24.6), while the remainder reported drinking at least monthly, including 23% drinking 2–3 times per week (95% CI: 22.2–24.2) and 18% drinking 4+ times per week (95% CI: 17.1–18.9). Among those who drank (N=6274), the most common typical quantity was about two drinks on a drinking day (39%, 95% CI: 37.5–40.1), although 13% reported five or more drinks (12.7%, 95% CI: 11.8–13.6). Heavier episodic drinking was frequent: among drinkers, 27% reported consuming three or more drinks weekly (95% CI: 25.6–28.0) and 22% reported daily or almost daily 3+ drinks (95% CI: 20.6–22.8). Alcohol use while selling sex was also widespread, with 48% reporting alcohol use during sex work in the past month (95% CI: 47.2–49.6), ranging from 33% in Lira to 69% in Kabale. Substantial district variation was observed in abstention, from 9% in Busia to 49% in Lira, indicating heterogeneous patterns of alcohol use across sites.

tables.title: Table P0: Pooled data for 15 districts-drug use among Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table O14: Mbarara Alcohol use among WCS, 2024-2025
Table O15: Tororo Alcohol use among WCS, 2024-2025
Result P: Drug use

Most women in commercial sex reported never using drugs, although 25% reported drug use in the past six months (95% CI: 24.3–26.4) and an additional 11% reported use more than six months ago (95% CI: 9.7–11.2). Among women with any history of drug use (N=2973), drug use while selling sex was common: 54% reported drug use during sex work in the past six months (95% CI: 51.9–55.9). Injection was also frequently reported among women with any drug use history, with 36% reporting injecting drugs in the past six months (95% CI: 33.8–37.7), and among those with any injection history (N=1551), 44% reported sharing injection equipment in the past six months (95% CI: 41.3–46.8). District variation was substantial for recent drug use, ranging from 15.9% in Hoima to 39.2% in Busia, and for recent injection among women with drug use history, ranging from 14.2% in Arua to 43–44% in Busia and Tororo. These findings indicate that while most women reported no drug use, drug use during sex work, injection, and injection equipment sharing were common among those reporting any drug use, with meaningful differences across districts.

tables.title: Table Q0: Pooled data for 15 districts-Depression among Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table P14: Mbarara drug use among WCS, 2024-2025
Table P15: Tororo drug use among WCS, 2024-2025
Result Q: Depression

Depressive symptoms were common among women in commercial sex. In pooled data, 73% reported having little interest or pleasure in doing things for at least several days in the past two weeks (27.4% “not at all”), and 77% reported feeling down, depressed, or hopeless for at least several days (23.0% “not at all”). Based on the PHQ-2 classification presented, 61% were categorized as having some or severe depression (95% CI: 59.3–61.6), while 22% had no or little depression (95% CI: 21.0–22.9) and 18% were undetermined (95% CI: 16.7–18.5). Among those classified as having some or severe depression (N=4984), 50% were further categorized as “likely depression” (49.7%, 95% CI: 48.1–51.2). District variation was substantial, including a high “undetermined” share in Lira (40%) and higher levels of “likely depression” among those with some/severe depression in Busia (73%), Kampala (67%), and Masaka (68%), compared with a much lower proportion in Buliisa (16%). In the past six months, the most commonly reported mental health experiences were depression (38%) and anxiety (31%), with smaller but notable proportions reporting experiences of stigma (20%) and rejection (20%).

tables.title: Table R0: Pooled data for 15 districts-Violence against children among Women who Engage in Commercial Sex, 2024-2025
context: Table Q14: Mbarara Depression among WCS, 2024-2025
Table Q15: Tororo Depression among WCS, 2024-2025
Result R: Violence against children

Among women in commercial sex who responded to the violence against children module (N=2164), 49% reported experiencing coerced sex during childhood (48.5%, 95% CI: 46.2–50.8) and 48% reported being physically forced to have sex (47.5%, 95% CI: 45.2–49.9). Among those reporting coerced/forced sex (N=1081), the most commonly reported perpetrators were boyfriends/spouses (32%) and neighbors (17%), while teachers (12%) and relatives/family members (11%) were also frequently reported. After violence, 35% reported not trying to seek professional help (95% CI: 31.4–37.7), while 23% sought help from a healthcare professional (95% CI: 20.1–25.6). Among those who did not seek help (N=365), the most commonly cited reasons were not knowing services were available (40%) and fear of getting in trouble (29%), followed by shame (16%) and reporting that services were not available (14%). District variation was substantial in childhood coerced sex, ranging from 28% in Arua to 66% in Busia, and in non–help-seeking after violence, ranging from 22% in Mbarara to 55% in Mbale, underscoring heterogeneous patterns of both violence exposure and access to formal support across districts.
